look_here_first: Look for LONG racemes arising in DISTINCT tiers or whorls along a flowering stem, sometimes with an upright terminal branch. The panicle can detach and tumble, but that fact and the head silhouette alone are not enough: mature spikelets should have longer awns than hooded windmillgrass, with fertile lemma awn around 4.8–9 mm and sterile lemma awn around 3.2–7 mm.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Accepted POWO species and Texas state-level native distribution; source-pool admission approved; three target-zone county confirmations not independently verified.

morphology_keys.habit: Perennial windmillgrass with ~10–16 racemes in separated whorls; ripe panicle may detach and tumble.
morphology_keys.spikelets: Fertile lemma awn ~4.8–9 mm; sterile lemma awn ~3.2–7 mm. Upper sterile floret is not a conspicuously swollen round hood.
best_field_traits: Awn measurements on fertile and sterile lemmas
Upright terminal branch and sometimes intact detachable head
crew_field_walkthrough: Use the whole held seedhead and/or the botanical illustration to locate the main vertical flowering axis.
Check whether long branches arise from more than one level along the axis; in photographs, overlapping branches can hide this, so document it with a clean side-on full head.
Dissect mature spikelets and measure the fertile-lemma and sterile-lemma awns SEPARATELY; head shape alone overlaps the hybrid.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole attached flowering stalk from below lowest whorl through terminal head, with metric scale.
Same-scale matched cucullata comparison showing crowded/looser whorl separation.
Individual fertile and upper sterile florets in macro with correctly assigned awns and mm scale.
Attached mature head vs fallen detachable panicle; basal crown and leaf ligule.
morphology_keys.field_photo_limitations: Separate photo lesson can include the original USDA botanical illustration, but it must be labeled as an ILLUSTRATION, not counted as a photo or as a measured modern specimen.
crew_field_steps: On an intact stalk, photograph the entire head from the lowest tier to highest; see whether rays attach at different heights.
In the existing hand-held photograph, longer narrow lateral racemes radiate from more than one height. Fingers give a rough scale, not a millimeter measurement.
Check the mature fertile and sterile lemmas separately. Current real pictures do not resolve an awn length or a single dissection.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Tumble windmillgrass tends to have separated tiers of longer (~5–15 cm) racemes and long awns. C. cucullata tends to have crowded shorter whorls and a swollen short-awned sterile hood. C. virgata often has one terminal feathery fan and a different fertile-lemma hair crown. The hybrid between cucullata and verticillata is a real confounder: never certify hybrid status from tier spacing.
comparisons.cautions: Head color, overall windmill appearance and awn length alone can mislead. Inspect a fully mature spikelet with scale; hybrid intermediates must remain uncertain.

diagnostic_image_needs: Whole mature head and basal crown with scale
Dissected mature fertile and sterile lemmas with millimeter scale
Matched local Chloris comparison showing diagnostic whorl and awn differences
Blade–sheath junction opened to show the TRUE ligule and collar with 1-mm scale; existing photographs do not show this organ.
Mature intact flowering axis photographed side-on from lowest to highest branch tier with attached stem and ruler; avoid mistaking overlapping branches for whorls.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: How to identify Chloris verticillata in the field
steps: Start with the two ACTUAL Joey Santore photographs of this grass: one shows tiered flowering racemes, the other gives leafy tuft context. The final reference is a historical USDA line illustration, NOT another field photograph.
On an intact stalk, photograph the entire head from the lowest tier to highest; see whether rays attach at different heights.
In the existing hand-held photograph, longer narrow lateral racemes radiate from more than one height. Fingers give a rough scale, not a millimeter measurement.
Check the mature fertile and sterile lemmas separately. Current real pictures do not resolve an awn length or a single dissection.
